item.title: Laying Out a Page From Scratch: Text Around a Floating Frame
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: How ODT, Word and RTF each say where a text box stands, how officeParser reads them into one shape, and how its PDF engine sets lines round the box, with an interactive column to try it.
item.content:encoded:
Reports and newsletters put boxes beside their text: a sidebar, a pull quote, a note in a shaded frame on the right while the paragraph runs down its left. Word calls it a text box, LibreOffice a frame. Until 8.3.0, officeParser read the box's text and put it in the flow, where it was drawn as one more paragraph. ODT's was worse: its text was glued to the paragraph it stood in, so the paragraph read Text in a floating frame on the right.A paragraph beside a floating text frame.

Putting the box back where it stands took two halves: reading where each format says the box is, and teaching the native PDF engine to set lines of text round it. This post is about both.

Three Formats, One Box

I made one document with one frame (2.2 inches wide, 1 inch tall, 4.2 inches from the left of the text column, at the top of its paragraph, with text running beside it) and saved it from LibreOffice as ODT, DOCX and RTF. Each says the same thing in its own units and its own words.

ODT writes the frame inside the paragraph it is anchored to, in inches, with how text goes round it in a graphic style: 

<text:p><draw:frame text:anchor-type="paragraph" svg:x="4.2in" svg:y="0in"
        svg:width="2.2004in" svg:height="1.0004in" draw:style-name="gr1">
    <draw:text-box><text:p>Text in a floating frame on the right.</text:p></draw:text-box>
</draw:frame>A paragraph beside a floating text frame. ...</text:p>

<style:graphic-properties style:wrap="parallel" style:horizontal-pos="from-left"
        style:horizontal-rel="paragraph" style:vertical-rel="paragraph" .../>

Word puts a drawing in a run of the paragraph, measured in EMUs (914,400 to the inch, 12,700 to the point), with what each offset is measured from: 

<wp:anchor distT="0" distB="0" distL="0" distR="0" ...>
  <wp:positionH relativeFrom="column"><wp:posOffset>3840480</wp:posOffset></wp:positionH>
  <wp:positionV relativeFrom="paragraph"><wp:posOffset>635</wp:posOffset></wp:positionV>
  <wp:extent cx="2011680" cy="914400"/>
  <wp:wrapSquare wrapText="bothSides"/>
  ... <wps:txbx><w:txbxContent> the box's paragraphs </w:txbxContent></wps:txbx>

RTF writes a shape in twips (twenty to the point), with its wrapping as a number and its colours as integers in blue, green, red order: 

{\shp{\*\shpinst\shpleft6048\shptop0\shpright9215\shpbottom1439\shpwr2
  {\sp{\sn fillColor}{\sv 13606770}}{\sp{\sn lineColor}{\sv 10773812}} ...
  {\shptxt Text in a floating frame on the right.\par}}}

3,840,480 EMUs, 6,048 twips and 4.2 inches are all 302.4 points. That agreement is the whole job of the readers: each turns its format's words into one shape, a drawing node holding the box's paragraphs, with ShapeMetadata.float saying where it stands. Here is what each of the three files reads as: 

import { parseOffice } from 'officeparser';

const ast = await parseOffice('layout.docx');
const frame = ast.content.find(node => node.type === 'drawing' && node.metadata?.float);
console.log(frame.metadata.float);
// {
//   horizontalFrom: 'column', verticalFrom: 'paragraph',
//   x: 302.4, y: 0.05, width: 158.4, height: 72, wrap: 'beside'
// }

The ODT gives x: 302.4 too (its sizes a fraction larger, as LibreOffice wrote them), and the RTF the same again, with the 9-point gap its shapes keep from text by default. The drawing node comes just before the paragraph it is anchored to, whichever format it came from. That order is what lets a writer place the box before it lays out the lines that go round it. Writers that have no place to put a box (Markdown, plain text, a spreadsheet) write its paragraphs where it stands, so no text is lost; with ignorePageGeometry, the box is read as it was before.

Setting Lines Round a Box

The native engine lays text out one line at a time, from the top of the page down. A box changes that in one place: before a line's first word is placed, the engine looks for boxes on the page that overlap the band the line will take, and works out how much room is left beside each.

  • Text takes the side with more room. A box near the right edge leaves the left for the text.
  • If that room is less than 36 points, or a third of the line, the line moves down below the box instead of squeezing a word or two into a sliver.
  • A box set to keep text above and below it (Word's wrapTopAndBottom, ODT's style:wrap="none") sends the line below it whatever the room.
  • A box set in front of or behind the text (Word's wrapNone) is drawn and the lines ignore it, as Word draws them.

Try it. Drag the box, or move it with the arrow keys, and change how text goes round it. This uses the same rules as the engine, and shows the float a reader would give for the box where you leave it:

What a Box Cannot Do

Text that is already on the page cannot go round anything. Most boxes are measured from their own paragraph, so the engine meets the box just before the lines that go round it. But a box can be measured from the page or the margin, or placed above its paragraph with a negative offset, and then it stands over lines the engine has already set. My first version simply drew it there, over them.

A review round I run before every release found that, and two more of the same family. A box whose text needed more than a page lost what did not fit, because a box belongs to one page. And a table starting just above a box grew down through it, because blocks other than text only checked for a box where they start. Now:

  • A box that would stand over text already laid out stands at its paragraph instead, so the text after it goes round it and nothing is hidden.
  • A box whose text is more than a page holds is set in the flow, all of it.
  • A table, a picture, code or a chart that would reach a box below it is measured first and starts below the box.
  • Footnotes at the foot of the page are not set round boxes.

Each of these trades a little fidelity for never losing text. A word processor would reflow the page so the earlier lines go round the box as well. A layout engine that sets lines once, top to bottom, cannot, and the honest answer is to move the box rather than cover what is there.

Where It Falls Short

  • Text goes down one side of a box. Word's wrapText="bothSides" can run text down both sides of a box in the middle of a column; officeParser uses the wider side.
  • A box aligned to the middle or bottom of its page or paragraph is placed at the top.
  • Pictures floating beside text (as opposed to text boxes) are still drawn in the flow.

The box above is the same document all the way through: read from ODT, Word or RTF, it comes out of the native engine with its paragraph running down its left, and as a paragraph of its own in formats that have no page to stand it on.

item.title: Reading the Spreadsheet You See, Not the One Stored
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: A cell stores 0.19 and shows 19%. What XLSX keeps, how Excel's number formats work, and how officeParser reads both halves of a cell so a CSV keeps the numbers and a PDF prints what the sheet shows.
item.content:encoded:
Type 19% into a spreadsheet cell and save the file. What is in the file is not "19%". It is 0.19, and a note elsewhere that says to show it as a percentage. A date is a count of days. Thirty hours is the number 1.25. A row you hid is still there, with a flag on it.

So which is the cell's content: what the file stores, or what the sheet shows? For years officeParser gave the stored value and nothing else, which is right for a CSV and wrong for a printout: a PDF of a budget that says 0.19 where everyone saw 19% is not the budget. In 8.3.0 a cell carries both, and every writer takes the one its format needs.

What an XLSX Cell Holds

I built a small workbook by hand, writing the XML myself so I knew exactly what was in it. One sheet, a label in column A and a value in column B. Here is the percentage, as the sheet stores it: 

<c r="B1" s="1"><v>0.19</v></c>

The s="1" is the only clue. It points into the workbook's list of cell styles, whose second entry says numFmtId="9", one of Excel's built-in formats: 0%. Formats of your own get numbers from 164 up and their code written out in the styles part: 

<numFmt numFmtId="164" formatCode="#,##0.00 [$€-407]"/>
<numFmt numFmtId="165" formatCode="dd.mm.yyyy"/>
<numFmt numFmtId="166" formatCode="#,##0.00;(#,##0.00)"/>
<numFmt numFmtId="169" formatCode="[h]:mm"/>

A format code is a small language. Sections split by semicolons are for positive numbers, negative numbers and zero, so #,##0.00;(#,##0.00) shows a debt in brackets without its minus sign. [$€-407] is a currency symbol with a locale tag. m is a month, unless it stands next to an hour or a second, when it is a minute. [h] counts hours past a day.

Both Halves of a Cell

officeParser reads each cell's stored value into its text, as before, and puts beside it what the sheet shows (shownText), what kind of value it is (valueType), the value in full where the text is something else (value), and the format code (numberFormat). A hidden row's cells are marked hidden. 

import { parseOffice } from 'officeparser';

const ast = await parseOffice('report.xlsx');
const sheet = ast.content.find(node => node.type === 'sheet');
for (const row of sheet.children) {
    for (const cell of row.children) console.log(cell.text, cell.metadata);
}

For the value column, that prints (the labels left out): 

0.19        { shownText: '19%', valueType: 'number', numberFormat: '0%' }
120         { shownText: '120.00 €', valueType: 'number', numberFormat: '#,##0.00 [$€-407]' }
2023-03-15  { shownText: '15.03.2023', valueType: 'date', value: '45000', numberFormat: 'dd.mm.yyyy' }
-1234.5     { shownText: '(1,234.50)', valueType: 'number', numberFormat: '#,##0.00;(#,##0.00)' }
06:00:00    { shownText: '6:00', valueType: 'time', value: '0.25', numberFormat: 'h:mm' }
10.456      { shownText: '10.5 kg', valueType: 'number', numberFormat: '0.0 "kg"', hidden: true }
30:00:00    { shownText: '30:00', valueType: 'time', value: '1.25', numberFormat: '[h]:mm' }
1E5         { valueType: 'text' }

A date's text is the ISO date, which every program reads the same way, and its value keeps the day count (45000 is 15 March 2023 in Excel's 1900 date system). The last cell is the reason valueType exists: 1E5 was typed as text, a part number perhaps, and a writer that guessed from the text alone would turn it into 100000.

Switch between the two halves of the same sheet, and show the hidden row:

Each Writer Takes Its Half

Having both lets every output take the half its format is for:

  • CSV, text and chunks keep the stored values. A CSV of the sheet starts Growth,0.19: a number another program can add up, not a string with a percent sign.
  • PDF prints what the sheet shows (19%, (1,234.50), 30:00) and leaves the hidden row out, as a printout does. pdfConfig.printHidden prints it.
  • XLSX output writes each format code as it was, so the value and its look survive a round trip.
  • ODS output writes the value as ODS holds one (a percentage, a currency amount, a date, a time of PT30H0M0S) with a number style built from the format code, and the shown text inside the cell, as ODS keeps it.
const pdf = await ast.to('pdf', { pdfConfig: { engine: 'native' } });                    // as seen
const all = await ast.to('pdf', { pdfConfig: { engine: 'native', printHidden: true } }); // hidden rows too

Writing the Shown Text

Excel's format codes are not a standard any library speaks, but officeParser already had an engine for something close: the template engine formats numbers and dates with Word's pictures (#,##0.00, dd.MM.yyyy). The spreadsheet reader turns what only Excel's codes hold into that language first: it picks the section for the value's sign, turns [$€-407] into its symbol, drops colours ([Red]) and locale tags, reads _) padding and * fill as a space, divides by a thousand for each trailing comma (#,##0,"K"), and decides whether each m is a month or a minute. Elapsed time ([h]:mm, [mm]:ss) it writes itself, which is how 1.25 days becomes 30:00 and not 6:00 on the next day.

What It Will Not Guess

Where a code says something officeParser cannot write the way Excel would, the cell gets no shown text and every output uses the stored value. That covers General, scientific notation (0.00E+00), fractions (# ?/?), conditions ([>=100]) and text sections. Excel's built-in date formats are left alone too, because they follow the date order of the machine that opens the file: what one reader sees as 3/15/2023 another sees as 15.03.2023, so the unambiguous ISO date is the better guess.

One more limit is easy to miss: the shown text uses a full stop for decimals and a comma for thousands. A format code says where the separators go, not which characters they are. Excel takes those from the machine's language, so a German Excel shows the price above as 120,00 €.

A spreadsheet is a table of numbers and a set of instructions for showing them. Read as one or the other, it is half a document. Read as both, a CSV can add it up and a PDF can print it as it was.

item.title: Drawing Hindi in a PDF: Glyph Positions, Conjuncts and /ActualText
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: Why a Hindi word came apart in officeParser's PDF writer, copied with its letters out of order, or drew the wrong glyphs, and the font and PDF details behind each failure.
item.content:encoded:
officeParser has a PDF writer of its own, the native engine, which draws a document with pdf-lib instead of a headless browser. Give it a font with pdfConfig.fallbackFonts and it will draw Greek, Arabic, Chinese or Hindi.

Hindi is where it went wrong, in three different ways at once. A word could come apart on the page. Copied out of the PDF, a word read with its letters out of order. And with some fonts every glyph was the wrong one. Each failure has its own cause, and none of them is in the code that lays out lines. This post is about those causes and what I changed for 8.3.0.

A Word is Not Written in the Order It is Drawn

Take the word हिंदी ("Hindi"). In Unicode it is five code points, in the order you type and say them: 

ह  U+0939  HA
ि  U+093F  VOWEL SIGN I
ं  U+0902  ANUSVARA
द  U+0926  DA
ी  U+0940  VOWEL SIGN II

The vowel sign ि comes after ह in the text but is drawn before it, to its left. The anusvara ं is a dot that sits above the letter before it and takes no room of its own. Other words go further: in क्ष, a letter, a virama and another letter become one glyph, a conjunct the font draws as a single shape.

Turning code points into glyphs and their places is shaping. A shaper reads the font's own tables (OpenType's GSUB and GPOS, or Apple's morx) and returns the glyphs in the order they are drawn, each with an advance and an offset. pdf-lib uses fontkit for this. For the word above, with Devanagari Sangam MN, fontkit returns the glyph for ि first, then ह, then the anusvara with no advance, then द and ी.

Failure One: the Positions Were Thrown Away

pdf-lib asks fontkit for that layout, but keeps only the glyph ids. The string it writes into the page is the glyphs one after another, and a PDF viewer moves each glyph along by the width the font file gives it, not by the advance the shaper worked out. Where the two agree, nothing shows. Where they do not (a mark the shaper sets at no advance, or a mark it moves sideways onto its letter), the marks stand in the wrong place and the word drifts apart.

The native engine now asks fontkit for the layout itself and writes it out whole: one string of glyphs (TJ), each moved from where the last one's width leaves off to where the shaper put it, with a rise (Ts) for a mark set above or below the line. Here is the word as it is written into the page now: 

/Span << /ActualText <FEFF0939093F090209260940> >> BDC
1 0 0 1 48 782.89 Tm
[ <0001> <0002> <0003> <0004> <0005> ] TJ
EMC

One string has another advantage over placing each glyph on its own: a program reading the PDF back measures the word as it is drawn. Placed glyph by glyph, a mark that the font gives a width but the shaper gives none made the word look as long as that, and the space after it disappeared when the text was read back.

Failure Two: Copying Gave the Glyphs, Not the Word

When you copy text from a PDF, the viewer does not have the text you typed. It has glyphs, and a table (ToUnicode) mapping each glyph back to characters. Map the glyphs of हिंदी in the order they are drawn and you get िहंदी: the vowel sign before its letter. That is what copying from the native engine's PDFs gave, and what any search over them found.

PDF has an answer for this, the same one browsers and LibreOffice use: wrap the glyphs in a marked-content span that carries the text they stand for, /ActualText. That is the BDC and EMC around the string above. The hex string is the word in UTF-16, in the order it is written. Poppler's pdftotext now reads the line as हिंदी हिन्दी नमस्ते क्षत्रिय श्री कृष्ण, exactly as typed.

Where the span goes matters

My first version closed the span after the text object (ET), and Poppler then read every word as standing at the origin of nothing: the words came out bottom-up, one a line. The span now opens and closes inside the text object, where a text position is current.

I did not mark right-to-left text the same way. Hebrew and Arabic glyphs are drawn in the order they are seen, each already mapped to its letter, and readers put them back in reading order themselves. Given an /ActualText for a Hebrew word, Poppler reversed it a second time. So Hebrew and Arabic are still drawn as pdf-lib draws them, and the shaped path is for the scripts of South and Southeast Asia and for letters with combining marks.

Failure Three: Some Fonts Drew the Wrong Glyphs

Fonts come with two kinds of outlines: TrueType (glyf) and CFF, the PostScript kind, in files that start with OTTO. The native engine subsets a font by default (pdfConfig.subsetFonts), embedding only the glyphs a document uses. For a TrueType font that works. For a CFF font, the subset fontkit writes is not one viewers can read: macOS Preview drew every glyph as another one, and Poppler reported the embedded font as invalid. This was not about Hindi at all. A Latin .otf came out as punctuation.

A CFF font is now embedded whole, labelled as the OpenType file it is. That uncovered a second bug: pdf-lib decides whether a font is CFF by asking fontkit for a cff property that the version it uses does not have, so a whole CFF font was declared as TrueType. And a font embedded whole had widths written only for the glyphs a character maps to directly. A conjunct, a ligature or the left-hand form of ि maps to no single character, so each of those took the PDF's default width of 1000 units. The engine now writes the widths, and the text mapping, for the glyphs it actually draws.

The cost is size. A whole font is the whole file, and a CFF font for Chinese or Japanese is large. If size matters, a TrueType font of the same family keeps the subsetting.

The Bug Found Along the Way: a Shaper That Never Returned

Reviewing the change, I tried a Devanagari word longer than a line. The engine breaks such a word between characters, and the process ran out of memory. The cause was not my code: given a vowel sign with no letter of its script before it, fontkit's shaper for Apple's morx tables never finishes. fontkit prefers morx to OpenType when a font has both, as some of the fonts that come with macOS do. A stray vowel sign is not exotic either: it is what you get when a word changes from bold to plain halfway through and each part is shaped on its own.

For such fonts the engine now lays out a vowel sign or virama with no letter of its script before it unshaped, as the glyph the font gives it, and shapes the text around it as usual. A word too long for a line is now cut between the characters a reader sees (grapheme clusters), never inside a syllable.

Reading It Back

officeParser reads PDFs too, with pdf.js, and the new PDFs found a gap there. pdf.js treats a glyph whose text holds a combining mark as a diacritic of no width. A conjunct's text holds a virama, so pdf.js measures क्ष as zero wide and puts the space before the word after the conjunct, inside the word's /ActualText span, where officeParser's reader dropped it along with the span's own text. A blank inside a span that lies before the span's glyphs is now read as the space before the word. The reader also composes an ActualText's marks with their letters when pdfParserConfig.normalizeText is on, as pdf.js does for the glyphs' text.

That was not the whole of it. pdf.js tells such a glyph by a regular expression, /^(\s)|(\p{Mn})|(\p{Cf})$/u, whose middle part has no anchors, so any glyph whose text holds a mark counts: a conjunct, and a syllable like ते too. It gives that glyph no advance and does not move past it, so the gap it measures to the next glyph starts from the wrong place. In a PDF that places each cluster on its own, as LibreOffice's do, that gap looked like a space, and words read back split: हिं दी for हिंदी. Since 8.4.0 the reader walks the page's drawing operators glyph by glyph, puts each piece of text where its glyphs are really drawn, and keeps a space only where the page draws one or leaves a gap. Words now read whole from LibreOffice's PDFs in the Indian languages and Thai I tested, and the space after a conjunct is kept.

Using It

import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { parseOffice } from 'officeparser';

const ast = await parseOffice('report.docx');
const pdf = await ast.to('pdf', {
    pdfConfig: {
        engine: 'native',
        fallbackFonts: [readFileSync('NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf')],
    },
});
writeFileSync('report.pdf', pdf.value);

Each character is drawn in the first font whose glyph for it draws something, so one Latin font in pdfConfig.fonts and a font for each other script in fallbackFonts covers a document that mixes them. A font may be a TrueType or OpenType file, and since 8.4.0 a WOFF or WOFF2 file too. The fonts need the optional peer dependency @pdf-lib/fontkit.

What is Still Not Right

  • Viewers built on pdf.js build their text from the glyphs, not from /ActualText, so copying there can still put ि before its letter.
  • Arabic and Hebrew marks are drawn where pdf-lib draws them: right for the fonts I tested, but not placed by the font's positioning table.

None of this was in the line breaking, the justification or the page layout. It was in the three places where text stops being text: when it becomes glyphs, when a viewer turns glyphs back into text, and when a font file is cut down to fit.

item.title: What is Actually Inside a .docx File? An Architectural Deep Dive
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: A tour of the .docx package: parts and relationships, runs that Word splits mid-word, lists stored in another file, merged cells, text boxes, and field codes, and what officeParser makes of them.
item.content:encoded:
If you rename any .docx file to .zip and unpack it, you do not find a simple text document. You find a small filesystem governed by ECMA-376 and ISO/IEC 29500, together known as Office Open XML (OOXML).

To read or write these files reliably, you have to look past what the editor shows and understand the data model underneath. Here is a tour of what is actually inside that archive, followed by what officeParser makes of it.

1. The Outer Shell: Open Packaging Conventions (OPC)

A .docx file is an Open Packaging Conventions (OPC) package: a ZIP archive holding data streams called parts, plus XML files called relationships that say how the parts refer to each other.

A minimal unpacked Word document looks roughly like this: 

my-document.docx/
├── [Content_Types].xml        # Content type of every part
├── _rels/
│   └── .rels                  # Package-level relationships
├── docProps/
│   ├── core.xml               # Title, author, created, modified
│   └── app.xml                # Application, page and word counts
└── word/
    ├── document.xml           # The main content
    ├── styles.xml             # Style hierarchy and defaults
    ├── numbering.xml          # List definitions
    ├── settings.xml           # Compatibility and editing settings
    ├── fontTable.xml          # Fonts the document uses
    ├── theme/
    │   └── theme1.xml         # Theme fonts and colours
    └── _rels/
        └── document.xml.rels  # Images, hyperlinks, headers, footers

Two structural patterns matter here:

  • Parts are found by relationship, not by path. The specification does not say the main text lives in word/document.xml. A strict consumer reads _rels/.rels and follows the relationship whose Type ends in /relationships/officeDocument. In practice Word and LibreOffice both write the main part at word/document.xml, and that is where officeParser looks for it.
  • Content types are declared. [Content_Types].xml gives the type of every part, by extension or by part name. Leave a part out and Word will usually report the file as corrupt.

2. The Content Core: WordprocessingML

The body of the document lives in word/document.xml. The root element is <w:document>, which holds one <w:body>. Inside the body, content is a sequence of block-level elements, mainly paragraphs (<w:p>) and tables (<w:tbl>).

The Fundamental Primitive: Runs (<w:r>)

A paragraph in Word is not a string with markup tags in it. It is a container of runs (<w:r>). A run is a stretch of text that shares one set of formatting properties.

Consider a sentence as simple as: "The quick brown fox." You might expect: 

<w:p>
  <w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The </w:t></w:r>
  <w:r>
    <w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr>
    <w:t>quick</w:t>
  </w:r>
  <w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> brown fox.</w:t></w:r>
</w:p>

Run Fragmentation

Word often does not produce runs that clean. If the user paused, fixed a typo, ran the spell checker, or moved the cursor away and back, the same sentence can come out in more pieces, with markers between them: 

<w:p>
  <w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The </w:t></w:r>
  <w:proofErr w:type="spellStart"/>
  <w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t>qui</w:t></w:r>
  <w:bookmarkStart w:id="0" w:name="_GoBack"/>
  <w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t>ck</w:t></w:r>
  <w:proofErr w:type="spellEnd"/>
  <w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> brown </w:t></w:r>
  <w:r><w:t>fox.</w:t></w:r>
</w:p>

The word "quick" is now two runs. Anything that searches one <w:t> at a time will miss it. This is also why a template placeholder such as {{customer_name}} so often fails to match: Word has stored it as {{cust, omer_, and name}} in three separate runs.

3. Numbering and Lists: The Disconnected Graph

Engineers coming from HTML or Markdown are usually surprised by how Word stores lists. In HTML a list is an explicit, self-contained element: <ol><li>First</li></ol>.

In WordprocessingML, there is no list element. Every list item is an ordinary paragraph whose properties (<w:pPr>) point into a separate file, word/numbering.xml. 

<!-- Inside word/document.xml -->
<w:p>
  <w:pPr>
    <w:numPr>
      <w:ilvl w:val="0"/>   <!-- Indent level 0 -->
      <w:numId w:val="2"/>  <!-- Numbering instance 2 -->
    </w:numPr>
  </w:pPr>
  <w:r><w:t>First bullet item</w:t></w:r>
</w:p>

To learn what bullet or number goes in front of that paragraph, a reader follows a three-step chain:

  1. Find <w:num w:numId="2"> in word/numbering.xml.
  2. Read its <w:abstractNumId w:val="4"/> pointer.
  3. Look up <w:abstractNum w:abstractNumId="4">, find the level <w:lvl w:ilvl="0">, and read its <w:numFmt> (for example bullet or decimal) and its <w:lvlText w:val="%1."/> template.

The file never says "this item is number 3". Items of one list can be separated by other paragraphs or tables, so a reader has to keep its own counters as it walks the document.

4. Tables: Grids, Merges, and Nesting

A Word table (<w:tbl>) declares a column grid (<w:tblGrid>), then rows (<w:tr>) of cells (<w:tc>).

Concept OOXML markup What it means
Column spans <w:gridSpan w:val="N"/> The cell covers N grid columns, like HTML colspan.
Vertical merges <w:vMerge w:val="restart"/>, then <w:vMerge/> There is no rowspan="N". The first row marks restart, and every row below repeats the cell with an empty <w:vMerge/>.
Unsplittable rows <w:cantSplit/> The row may not break across pages.
Nested tables <w:tc><w:tbl>...</w:tbl></w:tc> A cell can hold a whole table.

5. Text Boxes and Drawings: The Detached Canvas

Floating shapes and text boxes are one of the most common sources of missing text in simple extractors. A text box does not sit in the paragraph stream as text.

Word anchors a DrawingML element (<w:drawing>) or a legacy VML element (<w:pict>) inside a run, and the text sits deep inside it: 

<w:p>
  <w:r>
    <w:drawing>
      <wp:anchor>
        <a:graphic>
          <a:graphicData uri=".../word/2010/wordprocessingShape">
            <wps:wsp>
              <wps:txbx>
                <w:txbxContent>
                  <w:p>
                    <w:r><w:t>Text inside a floating box</w:t></w:r>
                  </w:p>
                </w:txbxContent>
              </wps:txbx>
            </wps:wsp>
          </a:graphicData>
        </a:graphic>
      </wp:anchor>
    </w:drawing>
  </w:r>
</w:p>

(The full namespace is http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape.) <w:txbxContent> is a nested document body with its own paragraphs, runs, and tables. An extractor that only walks the paragraphs directly under <w:body> misses every sidebar, callout, and caption drawn this way.

There is a second trap. For older readers, Word usually writes the same text box twice inside an <mc:AlternateContent> element: once as the modern shape, once as a VML fallback. An extractor that reads both branches returns the text twice.

6. Field Codes: The Inline State Machine

Page numbers, dates, cross-references, tables of contents, and some hyperlinks are fields. Word has two ways to write one:

  • Simple fields: <w:fldSimple w:instr="PAGE"> wraps the cached result in one element.
  • Complex fields: a sequence of runs marked by <w:fldChar>:
    1. <w:fldChar w:fldCharType="begin"/>
    2. <w:instrText>HYPERLINK "https://example.com"</w:instrText>
    3. <w:fldChar w:fldCharType="separate"/>
    4. Runs holding the cached visible text: <w:r><w:t>Visit site</w:t></w:r>
    5. <w:fldChar w:fldCharType="end"/>

Fields can nest (an IF field can contain a DATE field), so a reader has to track where each one begins and ends. An extractor that simply takes every text node in the XML returns the instruction (HYPERLINK "https://...") as if it were prose.

What officeParser Makes of All This

parseOffice reads the package and returns a typed tree, the same shape for every format the library supports: 

import { parseOffice } from 'officeparser';

const ast = await parseOffice('quarterly-report.docx');

ast.content;   // paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, ...
ast.metadata;  // title, author, created, modified, ...

const { value: markdown } = await ast.to('markdown');
const { value: chunks } = await ast.to('chunks');

Here is what the fragmented paragraph from section 2 becomes. This is real output: 

{
  "type": "paragraph",
  "text": "The quick brown fox.",
  "children": [
    { "type": "text", "text": "The ", "formatting": {} },
    { "type": "text", "text": "qui", "formatting": { "bold": true } },
    { "type": "text", "text": "ck", "formatting": { "bold": true } },
    { "type": "text", "text": " brown ", "formatting": {} },
    { "type": "text", "text": "fox.", "formatting": {} }
  ],
  "metadata": {}
}

I keep every run as its own text node, with its formatting, so nothing Word recorded is thrown away. The paragraph's own text is the joined string, so search and extraction never see the fragmentation. And the generators merge neighbours that share formatting: ast.to('markdown') writes that paragraph as The **quick** brown fox.

For the rest of the tour:

  • Lists become list nodes carrying listId, listType, indentation, and itemIndex. The index keeps counting when a list is interrupted by an ordinary paragraph, so numbering stays correct.
  • Tables follow table, row, cell, with rowSpan and colSpan worked out from vMerge and gridSpan. A cell can hold another table.
  • Text boxes, content controls, and SmartArt are read where they stand, after the paragraph that draws them. Of the two copies in an AlternateContent, one is read.
  • Headings come from the paragraph style (Heading1, Title, and so on).
  • Tracked changes: inserted text is read, text deleted or moved away is not.
  • Templates: OfficeTemplate.render fills {{placeholders}} even when Word has split one across several runs.

It does not cover every corner of a specification that runs to more than 6,000 pages. The capability matrix in the README lists what each format gives you, and a separate article covers the jobs officeParser is the wrong tool for.

item.title: How PowerPoint Really Stores a Slide: Coordinate Systems, Master Trees, and DrawingML
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: Why a slide is a canvas and not a text flow: English Metric Units, the theme, master and layout chain, the shape tree, speaker notes, and why reading order is hard.
item.content:encoded:
Developers building document pipelines often treat PowerPoint (.pptx) as "Word with page breaks". That assumption is where broken text extraction, scrambled reading order, and lost speaker notes come from.

PresentationML describes a layout, not a flow. Text does not exist on its own as prose. It exists inside shapes that are placed on a canvas.

1. The Four-Tier Inheritance Tree

Open the XML of a slide, say ppt/slides/slide1.xml, and you will often find text with no font size, no font family, no bold flag, and no colour.

PowerPoint knows how to draw it because each slide sits at the bottom of a four-level chain: 

Theme (theme1.xml)
└── Slide Master (slideMaster1.xml)
    └── Slide Layout (slideLayout2.xml)
        └── Slide (slide1.xml)

A shape marked <p:ph type="title"/> is a placeholder. It takes its position and text formatting from the matching placeholder in its layout. The layout takes its defaults from the master. The master takes its colours (accent1, tx1) and fonts (majorFont, minorFont) from the theme.

What this means for a parser

A reader that looks only at slide1.xml cannot tell whether a title is 32pt bold or 14pt italic. To know how the text looks, it has to follow the relationships back through the layout, the master, and the theme.

2. The EMU: Why 914,400?

Open any shape in a slide's XML and the coordinates look absurdly large: 

<a:xfrm>
  <a:off x="1524000" y="914400"/>    <!-- X and Y offsets -->
  <a:ext cx="6096000" cy="1828800"/> <!-- Width and height -->
</a:xfrm>

These are EMUs (English Metric Units). OOXML did not invent the unit. Office's older binary drawing format already measured in EMUs, and OOXML kept it.

The number was chosen so that the units people actually design in all come out as whole numbers:

  • 1 inch = 914,400 EMUs
  • 1 cm = 360,000 EMUs
  • 1 mm = 36,000 EMUs
  • 1 point = 12,700 EMUs
  • 1 pixel at 96 DPI = 9,525 EMUs

One EMU is about 28 nanometres. Because an inch, a centimetre, a point, and a pixel are each a whole number of EMUs, a layout can be stored in integers and converted between units without rounding drift.

3. The Shape Tree (p:spTree)

Everything on a slide sits in its <p:spTree> (shape tree): 

<p:sld>
  <p:cSld>
    <p:spTree>
      <p:sp>...</p:sp>            <!-- Shape or text box -->
      <p:grpSp>...</p:grpSp>      <!-- Group of shapes -->
      <p:graphicFrame>...</p:graphicFrame> <!-- Table or chart -->
      <p:pic>...</p:pic>          <!-- Picture -->
    </p:spTree>
  </p:cSld>
</p:sld>

DrawingML: The Shared Graphics Language

In Word, text is WordprocessingML (w:p, w:r, w:t). In PowerPoint, text is DrawingML (a:p, a:r, a:t), held in a shape's text body: 

<p:sp>
  <p:spPr>
    <a:xfrm>
      <a:off x="457200" y="457200"/>
      <a:ext cx="8229600" cy="1143000"/>
    </a:xfrm>
    <a:prstGeom prst="rect"><a:avLst/></a:prstGeom>
  </p:spPr>
  <p:txBody>
    <a:bodyPr anchor="t"/>
    <a:p>
      <a:r>
        <a:rPr sz="2800" b="1"/> <!-- 28pt bold -->
        <a:t>Slide Title Text</a:t>
      </a:r>
    </a:p>
  </p:txBody>
</p:sp>

Font size (sz) is in hundredths of a point, so 2800 is 28pt. A table lives in a <p:graphicFrame> as an <a:tbl>, and each of its cells has its own text body.

4. Reconstructing Reading Order from a 2D Canvas

This is the hardest problem in reading presentations: reading order.

If a slide has a title, a left column, and a right column, in what order do they appear in the XML?

The order of the shape tree is the stacking order, back to front. That usually follows the order in which the shapes were created, changed by any "Send to Back" or "Bring to Front". A title that was deleted and added again late can easily be the last element in <p:spTree>.

There are three common strategies, and none is free:

Strategy How it works Where it fails
Document order Read shapes in the order the XML lists them. A title or caption can come out after the text it belongs with.
Placeholder priority Put type="title" first, then type="body". Does nothing for plain text boxes, which are not placeholders.
Spatial sorting Group shapes into horizontal bands by their Y position, then sort each band left to right. Overlapping shapes, diagrams, and columns of unequal height have no single right answer.

5. Speaker Notes: The Detached Stream

Often the most useful text in a presentation is not on the slide at all. It is in the speaker notes.

PowerPoint does not store notes inside the slide. Instead, ppt/slides/_rels/slide1.xml.rels holds a relationship pointing to ../notesSlides/notesSlide1.xml.

A notes slide is a small slide of its own. It has one shape that shows a thumbnail of the slide it belongs to, and another (a placeholder of type="body") holding the notes text.

How officeParser Reads a Presentation

Here is what the library does as of version 8.1.1, and what it does not.

  1. Each slide becomes a slide node, in the order the presentation's slide list shows them. A slide's slideNumber is its place in the deck, not the number in its file name.
  2. A title placeholder (title or ctrTitle) becomes a level-1 heading. Other text becomes paragraphs and lists.
  3. Tables, charts (with their data), pictures, SmartArt text, and comments are read.
  4. Speaker notes are attached to the slide that names them, as slide.notes. Set ignoreNotes: true to leave them out.
  5. Slide masters are kept apart in ast.auxiliary.slideMasters, so their boilerplate does not mix into the slides.
import { parseOffice } from 'officeparser';

const ast = await parseOffice('pitch-deck.pptx');

for (const slide of ast.content) {
    const title = slide.children?.find(n => n.type === 'heading');
    console.log(title?.text, '| notes:', slide.notes?.length ?? 0);
}

const { value: markdown } = await ast.to('markdown');

In the Markdown, slides are separated by ---, the title is a # heading, and each speaker note is a block quote that starts with > **Note:**.

Two honest limits

Reading order is document order. officeParser reads shapes in the order the file lists them and marks titles as headings. It does not re-sort shapes by position, so a slide whose shape tree is out of visual order comes out in that order.

Inherited formatting is not resolved. Formatting comes from the slide's own XML. A font size or colour that a slide inherits from its layout, master, or theme is not filled in.

item.title: Why PDF Text Extraction is Unforgivingly Hard
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: A PDF has no words, paragraphs, or reading order. Positioned glyphs, missing spaces, font encodings, ligatures, multi-column pages, and the XY-cut that rebuilds reading order.
item.content:encoded:
Every engineer who sets out to pull text from a PDF starts with optimism: "How hard can it be? It's just text and images on a page."

Two weeks later they are deep in transformation matrices, font encoding tables, kerning adjustments, and scrambled multi-column layouts.

Adobe introduced PDF in 1993 with one goal: a page should look the same on every screen and every printer. It was not designed to be reflowed, searched, or read by a machine. Here is what is actually going on inside a PDF content stream.

1. PDF Has No Words, Lines, or Paragraphs

In HTML, Word, or Markdown, text sits in containers that say what it is: 

<p>The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.</p>

In PDF, none of these concepts exist. A content stream is a list of drawing commands, in a notation that comes from PostScript: 

BT                  % Begin a text object
/F1 12 Tf           % Select font F1 at 12pt
1 0 0 1 72 710 Tm   % Text matrix: position at x=72, y=710
(The) Tj            % Show the glyphs "The"
30 0 Td             % Move 30 units to the right
(quick) Tj          % Show the glyphs "quick"
ET                  % End the text object

Notice what is missing:

  • Nothing says (The) and (quick) are in the same paragraph.
  • Nothing says they are on the same line.
  • Nothing says what order they should be read in.

2. The Missing Spaces

In a text file, words are separated by space characters. In a PDF, the space is often not stored at all.

Typesetting software positions glyphs precisely with the TJ operator, which mixes strings with numeric adjustments: 

[(T) 12 (h) -5 (i) 2 (s) -250 (i) 4 (s) -250 (P) 10 (D) -3 (F)] TJ

The numbers are in thousandths of the font size, and a positive number moves the next glyph back. So -250 means "move forward by a quarter of the font size before the next letter".

To a human, that gap is a space between words. To a naive extractor there is no space character anywhere, and the result is ThisisPDF.

A threshold, not a fact

Every PDF extractor has to guess where the spaces are. The usual rule is a threshold: if the gap between two fragments is wider than some fraction of the font size, insert a space. Set it too high and words run together. Set it too low and kerning splits single words apart. In officeParser that fraction is pdfParserConfig.spaceToleranceFactor, and it defaults to 0.25.

3. Font Encodings: Why Copied Text Comes Out as Gibberish

Have you ever copied text out of a PDF and pasted nonsense?

A PDF does not have to store Unicode. To save space, PDF producers subset fonts: they embed only the glyphs the document uses, and they are free to number those glyphs however they like:

  • Code 0x01 → the glyph for "E"
  • Code 0x02 → the glyph for "T"
  • Code 0x03 → the glyph for "O"

On screen the page shows "ETO". The bytes in the file are 1, 2, and 3.

The ToUnicode CMap

For such a font to be searchable, the producer embeds a ToUnicode CMap that maps each code back to Unicode: 

/CIDInit /ProcSet findresource begin
12 dict begin
begincmap
1 begincodespacerange
<0000> <FFFF>
endcodespacerange
1 beginbfrange
<0001> <0001> <0045>   % Code 0x0001 is U+0045 ("E")
endbfrange
endcmap

A font that uses a standard encoding can still be decoded without one. But when a subset font has neither a usable encoding nor a ToUnicode map, or the map is wrong, the text layer cannot be recovered. The only way to get the words back is to render the page and run OCR on it.

4. Ligatures: When Two Letters Become One Glyph

Good typography joins certain letter pairs into one shape: "ff", "fi", "fl", "ffi", and "ffl".

In a PDF a ligature is drawn as a single glyph. Unicode has code points for these five (U+FB00 to U+FB04, in the Alphabetic Presentation Forms block), and a PDF may map the glyph to one of them. So the word "financial" can arrive as ﬁnancial, with the single character U+FB01 at the front.

Unless the extractor expands those back to plain letters, a search for "financial" will not match the document.

5. The 2D Layout Problem: The Multi-Column Trap

Take an ordinary two-column page: 

+------------------+------------------+
| (1) The quarter's| (3) Next year's  |
| (2) revenue grew.| (4) plans hold.  |
+------------------+------------------+

A parser that sorts text by vertical position reads straight across the gutter:

  1. y = 700: (1) The quarter's (left column)
  2. y = 700: (3) Next year's (right column)
  3. y = 680: (2) revenue grew. (left column)
  4. y = 680: (4) plans hold. (right column)

The result reads: "The quarter's Next year's revenue grew. plans hold."

The Fix: Recursive XY-Cut

The classic way to recover reading order is the XY-cut:

  1. Project every text box onto the horizontal axis.
  2. Look for a vertical band where no text falls (a gutter).
  3. If there is a clear one, cut the page into a left part and a right part.
  4. Do the same on the vertical axis to cut each part into horizontal bands.
  5. Repeat inside every piece until nothing more can be cut. Then read the pieces in order.

The hard part is deciding what counts as a gutter. Cut too eagerly and a wide gap between two words reorders a sentence. In officeParser a vertical cut needs a gap that runs the full height of the block.

What officeParser Does with a PDF

officeParser does not decode PDFs from scratch. It uses Mozilla's pdf.js to read content streams, fonts, and CMaps, and builds the layout reconstruction on top:

  • Lines and spaces. Fragments are grouped into lines and spaces are inserted from the gaps between them (lineToleranceFactor, spaceToleranceFactor).
  • Reading order. Multi-column pages are read with a recursive XY-cut (detectColumns, on by default).
  • Words. Words hyphenated across a line break are joined (mergeHyphenatedWords), and ligatures are expanded (normalizeText).
  • Structure. When a PDF is tagged, headings, tables, lists, and footnotes come from its tag tree (useTags). When it is not, they are recovered from geometry.
  • OCR. Scanned pages have no text layer. OCR (Tesseract) is opt-in, and runs over the images extracted from the pages.
import { parseOffice } from 'officeparser';

const ast = await parseOffice('research-paper.pdf', {
    pdfParserConfig: {
        detectColumns: true,         // recursive XY-cut (default)
        mergeHyphenatedWords: true,  // default
        spaceToleranceFactor: 0.25,  // default
    },
    // For scanned documents, OCR the page images:
    extractAttachments: true,
    ocr: true,
    onWarning: issue => console.warn(issue.code, issue.message),
});

const { value: markdown } = await ast.to('markdown');
Where it is best-effort

Structure recovered from geometry is a guess. In an untagged PDF, a table, or text floated beside a figure, may not separate perfectly. Underline and strikethrough are not extracted, because a PDF draws them as separate lines.

The parser tells you when it suspects trouble: PDF_NO_TEXT_EXTRACTED when a document yields almost no text and OCR is off, and PDF_TEXT_ENCODING_SUSPECT when a fifth or more of the characters it read (out of at least 50) could not be mapped to Unicode.

item.title: Security War Stories: Decompression Bombs, SSRF, and Hardening an Office Parser
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: Four holes found and fixed in officeParser: a ZIP header that lies about its size, SSRF through PDF rendering, spreadsheet repeat attributes, and nesting that runs the stack out.
item.content:encoded:
When your application accepts uploaded Word documents, spreadsheets, or PDFs, it is not just reading text. It is running an interpreter over files that someone else built, and that someone may be an adversary.

These are four problems I found and fixed in officeParser. For each one: how the attack works, what the library used to do, and what it does now. All four are in the changelog.

War Story 1: The ZIP Header That Lies

Every modern office document (.docx, .pptx, .xlsx, .odt) is a ZIP archive, so decompression is the first code an upload reaches.

The classic threat is the decompression bomb. The well-known 42.zip is 42 kilobytes and unpacks, through layers of nested archives, to 4.5 petabytes. Nesting is not even needed: in 2019 David Fifield showed that a single non-recursive archive can reach a ratio above 28 million to one by making its files overlap.

Why Checking the Header Fails

The obvious defence is to read the uncompressed size from the ZIP header and refuse anything too big: 

// Looks safe. Is not.
if (entry.uncompressedSize > 50 * 1024 * 1024) {
    throw new Error('File too big');
}

That field is written by whoever made the archive. An attacker declares 1,024 bytes and ships a DEFLATE stream that inflates to gigabytes. The parser trusts the header, starts inflating into memory, and the process dies.

officeParser used to make exactly this mistake: its size limit was checked against the declared size.

What officeParser Does Now

Archives are inflated as a stream, and the limit is applied to the bytes that actually come out. The moment the running total crosses the limit, extraction stops with ZIP_SIZE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED. The number of entries is capped too (ZIP_ENTRY_COUNT_LIMIT_EXCEEDED). Both limits are yours to tighten: 

const ast = await parseOffice(upload, {
    decompressionLimits: {
        maxUncompressedBytes: 64 * 1024 * 1024, // default: 512 MB
        maxZipEntries: 2000,                    // default: 10,000
    },
});

Entries are held in memory and never written to disk by the library, so a path-traversal name such as ../../etc/passwd has nowhere to go.

War Story 2: SSRF Through PDF Rendering

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) means tricking a server into making a request the attacker could not make directly. The usual target is something only the server can reach, such as an internal service or the cloud metadata address 169.254.169.254, which on a carelessly configured instance hands out credentials.

How a Document Carries the Request

Documents are full of URLs. A Word file can point an image at an external address: 

<!-- Inside word/_rels/document.xml.rels -->
<Relationship Id="rId9"
    Type=".../relationships/image"
    Target="http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
    TargetMode="External"/>

HTML does the same with <img src="...">. None of this matters while the URL stays a string. It matters the moment something fetches it.

officeParser's parsers never fetch a URL found in a document. A remote image stays a URL in the AST. The hole was on the output side. The default PDF engine builds HTML from the document and renders it in headless Chromium through Puppeteer. Chromium did what browsers do: it loaded every image and stylesheet the HTML referenced, from the server it was running on.

What officeParser Does Now

The PDF generator intercepts every request the page makes. Inline data: and blob: URIs are allowed, and so is the one host configured for the chart library. Everything else is aborted, and a warning reports that a remote resource was blocked. It blocks all remote loads and does not try to filter by address. A filter for "internal" addresses is easy to get wrong, and a converted PDF has no need to reach the network.

Links are handled separately. On output, a document's link targets pass through a scheme allowlist (http, https, mailto, tel, and relative links), so a javascript: link in an uploaded file does not survive into generated HTML.

War Story 3: A Few Hundred Bytes, Millions of Cells

OpenDocument has an attribute for compressing runs of identical cells: 

<table:table-row>
  <table:table-cell><text:p>Start</text:p></table:table-cell>
  <table:table-cell table:number-columns-repeated="1048576"/>
</table:table-row>

It exists for a good reason. LibreOffice routinely writes table:number-rows-repeated="1048566" to say "the rest of the sheet is empty". But a parser that takes the number at its word runs this: 

for (let i = 0; i < repeated; i++) {
    row.cells.push(new Cell());
}

Rows repeat too, and the two multiply. The ZIP limits cannot help, because the XML is tiny and the expansion happens later, while the tree is being built. officeParser expanded these attributes without a bound, so a few hundred bytes could ask for millions of nodes. After I fixed that for sheets, the same attribute turned up in a chart's embedded table: a 1.3 KB document that repeated one cell 100,000,000 times ended the process out of memory.

The fix could not be "cap the attribute", because that breaks real spreadsheets. What is bounded instead is what gets built:

  • A document may materialize at most maxTableCells cells (default 1,000,000, plus one for each byte of the file, so a large real spreadsheet is not cut short). Past that the parser clamps and warns once.
  • A repeated empty cell builds nothing and is skipped in one step. Looping over it was a CPU attack of its own.
  • Repeated rows and columns share their child nodes; they are not deep copies.
  • maxRepeatedContent (default 16,777,216 characters, plus 16 for each byte of the file) bounds the total content a document may repeat by reference.

War Story 4: Nesting That Runs the Stack Out

XML lets elements nest, and an attacker can nest the same element thousands deep: 

<w:p>
  <w:hyperlink>
    <w:hyperlink>
      <w:hyperlink>
        ... thousands of levels ...
      </w:hyperlink>
    </w:hyperlink>
  </w:hyperlink>
</w:p>

This one bit twice. The first problem was time. Every level of nested hyperlink applied its link to every run inside it, so the work grew with depth times runs. A 23 KB file with 1,000 levels around 400,000 runs took 17 seconds. Now the outermost hyperlink applies its link once.

The second problem was the call stack. A recursive reader that goes deep enough throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, and until 8.1.0 that surfaced as a generic "file corrupted" error. How deep is "deep enough" is not a constant. It depends on the engine, the stack size, and even on whether the code has been optimized yet. On Node 25 I measured this traversal running out somewhere between 900 and 1,000 levels in a fresh process.

The 512-level guard

Since 8.1.1 the Word parser counts depth inside a paragraph and stops at 512 levels, well before the stack is at risk. HTML has had a 256-level cap since 7.4.0, and RTF since 8.1.0. Other deep nesting, such as tables inside table cells, still relies on catching the stack overflow. Either way the caller gets the same typed error: 

try {
    await parseOffice(upload);
} catch (err) {
    if (err.officeIssue?.code === 'MAX_NESTING_DEPTH_EXCEEDED') {
        // The input was built to be deep. Reject it.
    }
}

The Baseline, and Its Limits

Beyond those four stories, this is what the library does as a matter of course:

  • Every generator escapes what it writes. Document text is attacker-controlled, so each output has its own escaping: HTML and CSS, URLs, RTF control words, LaTeX commands, Markdown, and CSV formulas.
  • Limits apply to real work, not declared sizes: inflated bytes, ZIP entries, table cells, XML elements, and repeated content.
  • Prototype pollution is closed. A list id of __proto__ in a crafted document once reached Object.prototype through a counter map. Those maps now have no prototype, and the keys __proto__, constructor, and prototype are never copied from a caller's config.
  • The security suite has more than 1,200 checks in test/security/testSanitization.ts. It is part of npm test, which CI runs on every push to master and on every pull request against it.

None of that is a guarantee. I am the sole maintainer, and a parser this size has attack surface I have not found yet. If you process untrusted files, run the parse somewhere you can afford to lose: a worker or container with memory and time limits and low privileges. Use decompressionLimits and abortSignal. Do not rely on any one library's hardening as your whole defence.

item.title: From String Scraping to AST: The Architectural Evolution of officeParser
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: Why returning one flat string hit a ceiling, and how a typed AST made conversion between Office, Markdown, HTML, and LaTeX possible.
item.content:encoded:
Every library starts with a narrow problem. I wrote the first version of officeParser in 2019 to do one thing: get the text out of Word and PowerPoint files in Node.js, with no LibreOffice to install, no Python to spawn, and no Java bridge.

That first version did exactly that and nothing more. It unzipped the file, parsed document.xml, collected every piece of text it found, and joined the pieces with spaces. You got one flat string.

It was small and it solved the immediate need. Excel and OpenDocument support followed within a week. For years, a flat string was the whole product. Then documents started feeding search indexes and language models, and the flat string became a dead end.

What a Flat String Loses

Consider what happens when you reduce a financial report or a contract to one string:

  • Tables collapse. The cells of a five-column balance sheet become a run of numbers, and which number belonged to which row and column is gone.
  • The outline disappears. A chapter title looks the same as a bullet point three levels down.
  • Links and references vanish. A hyperlink keeps its words and loses its target. A footnote lands wherever the file happened to store it.
  • Code and math lose their edges. Nothing marks where a formula starts or stops.
Why this matters more with LLMs

A language model leans on structure: headings, lists, and tables tell it what belongs together. Hand it a table flattened into a line of numbers and it has to guess which figure answers the question. The information was in the document. The extraction threw it away.

The Pivot: Documents as Compilers See Them

The way out was to stop treating this as a string problem and treat it as a compiler problem.

A compiler does not translate source code to machine code with search and replace. It parses the source into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) that captures what the program means, independent of how it was written down.

Documents work the same way. A table may be written as WordprocessingML (<w:tbl>), OpenDocument (<table:table>), HTML (<table>), Markdown (| col |), or LaTeX (\begin{tabular}). The thing being described is the same every time: rows of cells.

The Shape of the Tree

Version 6 (January 2026) replaced the string with a tree. Every parser returns the same structure: 

OfficeParserAST
├── type         'docx' | 'pptx' | 'pdf' | 'md' | ... (14 formats)
├── metadata     title, author, created, modified, ...
├── content      OfficeContentNode[]
├── auxiliary    headers, footers, slide masters, PDF outline
├── attachments  images and charts (with extractAttachments)
├── warnings     non-fatal issues found while parsing
└── to(format)   generate another format from this tree

Each content node has a type, its text, its children, and optional formatting and metadata. The node types are a closed set: 

type OfficeContentNodeType =
    | 'paragraph' | 'heading' | 'list' | 'text' | 'break' | 'code'
    | 'table' | 'row' | 'cell'
    | 'image' | 'chart' | 'drawing' | 'embed'
    | 'slide' | 'sheet' | 'page' | 'slideMaster'
    | 'note' | 'comment' | 'header' | 'footer'
    | 'admonition'
    | 'definitionList' | 'definitionTerm' | 'definitionDescription';

A table is always table, then row, then cell, whichever format it came from. Footnotes and speaker notes hang off the node that refers to them (node.notes), and so do comments (node.comments).

Hub and Spoke: Why Generation Came Next

Once every format parses into one tree, conversion stops being a matrix. Without a shared tree, converting between formats means writing a translator for every pair: 

DOCX -> Markdown     PPTX -> Markdown
DOCX -> HTML         PDF  -> HTML
ODT  -> DOCX         ... one per pair

With the tree in the middle, each format needs at most two pieces: a parser that produces the tree and a generator that consumes it. 

DOCX   PPTX   PDF   Markdown   LaTeX
   \     |     |      |        /
    v    v     v      v       v
        [ OfficeParserAST ]
    /    |     |      |       \
   v     v     v      v        v
DOCX   HTML   PDF   Markdown   chunks

Version 7.0 (May 2026) added the generators, the chunker for retrieval pipelines, and parsers for Markdown, HTML, and CSV. Version 8.0 added native DOCX and ODT output and a PDF engine that needs no browser. Version 8.1 added LaTeX in both directions.

Today that is 14 input formats and 11 outputs. Pair by pair, it would be 154 converters. With the tree, it is 14 parsers and 11 generators, and a new parser can be written to every existing output on the day it lands.

The Round-Trip Rule

Generation brought a rule I now hold every feature to:

A feature is not done until it round-trips

What a parser captures, the matching generator must be able to write back. The test suite checks it directly: parse a sample, generate the same format from the tree, parse the result, and compare what the two trees hold.

That rule is about one format at a time. Across formats, conversion is only as lossless as the target allows. Markdown has no merged cells, so a table with spans is written as an HTML table inside the Markdown. Plain text has no links. Where a target cannot say something, the generator falls back to the closest thing it can say.

Holding to the rule surfaced a long list of details that a text extractor never has to care about:

  • Merged cells (rowSpan, colSpan) surviving between Word, OpenDocument, and HTML tables.
  • List numbering that keeps counting when a list is interrupted by an ordinary paragraph.
  • Bookmarks and heading anchors (anchorIds), so internal links still land.
  • Guarding formula characters in CSV output without corrupting cells that are just negative numbers.

No Office Suite Required

One constraint from 2019 is still in place: parsing needs nothing but the npm package. There is no LibreOffice, no Java, and no Python behind it.

Parsing is JavaScript all the way down. PDF reading uses pdf.js, and OCR uses Tesseract compiled to WebAssembly. That is also why the same code runs in a browser, from a bundle of about 6 MB, so a file can be parsed without leaving the user's machine.

There is one place where I traded that purity for fidelity, and it is opt-out. The default PDF output engine renders through headless Chromium (Puppeteer, an optional peer dependency), because a browser's layout engine gives the most faithful page. If you do not want a browser, the native engine writes PDF directly with pdf-lib, with simpler layout, in the standard PDF fonts or in fonts you give it.

Trade-off Wrapping an office suite officeParser
Install System packages, fonts, and a process to manage One npm package
Runs in the browser No Yes
Page layout fidelity High: it runs a real layout engine Structure, not pixels
What you get back A converted file A typed tree you can inspect, filter, and convert

The third row is a real cost. Where officeParser is the wrong tool covers it and the other jobs this design does not do.

Looking Back

Moving from a string to a tree was not a refactor. It changed what the library is for. Reading a .docx, turning Markdown into a Word report, and chunking a PDF for retrieval look like three features. They are one tree with different things attached to each end.

item.title: Where officeParser is the Wrong Tool: An Honest Engineering Guide
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: The jobs officeParser does not do: PDFs that match Word exactly, formula recalculation, legacy .doc files, formulas and native charts in what it writes, macros, and TeX typesetting, and what to use instead.
item.content:encoded:
Every architecture is a set of trade-offs. When I designed officeParser, I made three on purpose:

  • I chose an npm package with no office suite behind it over wrapping a desktop application.
  • I chose structure and meaning over reproducing how a page looks in print.
  • I chose running in both Node.js and the browser over features that would need a native rendering engine.

Those choices make officeParser a good fit for document ingestion, format conversion, and client-side processing. They also mean there are jobs it cannot do, and it is better that you hear that from me than discover it in production.

If your project needs any of the following, use something else.

1. You Need a PDF That Matches Word Exactly

Suppose the requirement is: "I have a contract in Word. I need a PDF with the same line breaks and the same page breaks that Word would produce."

officeParser cannot do this.

Where Word breaks a line or a page is not written in the file. It is computed by Word's layout engine from font metrics, kerning, and its own rules. officeParser models what a document says: headings, paragraphs, tables, lists, formatting. Its PDF output lays that structure out again, through a browser engine or its own simpler one. The content will be right. The page breaks will not be Word's.

What to use instead
  • Word itself, or Microsoft's own conversion through the Graph API. Only Word's engine reproduces Word.
  • LibreOffice in headless mode: soffice --headless --convert-to pdf document.docx. Close to Word, though not identical, and it needs the document's fonts installed.
  • Gotenberg: a Docker service that wraps LibreOffice and Chromium behind an HTTP API.

2. You Need a Spreadsheet That Recalculates

Suppose the requirement is: "Load a workbook, change cell B4, and have every formula that depends on it update."

officeParser is not a calculation engine.

When it reads an .xlsx file, it reads the values: for a formula cell, the result Excel computed and saved the last time the file was written. It does not read the formula text and it does not evaluate anything, so an .xlsx it writes back out holds the values, not the formulas (see section 4).

What to use instead
  • HyperFormula: a headless spreadsheet engine in TypeScript, from the Handsontable team, with a dependency graph and several hundred built-in functions.
  • ExcelJS: reads and writes workbooks, including formulas and styling. It does not calculate either.
  • Apache POI (Java): workbook manipulation with a formula evaluator.

3. You Have Legacy Binary Files (.doc, .xls, .ppt)

The pre-2007 Office formats are a different family: binary records inside a compound file, not XML in a ZIP. officeParser reads the modern formats (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx), OpenDocument, PDF, RTF, and the text formats. It does not read .doc, .xls, or .ppt.

If you have an archive of old files, convert them first. LibreOffice does this well: soffice --headless --convert-to docx old-file.doc. Then parse the result.

4. You Need Formulas or Native Charts in the Files You Write

Since 8.3.0, officeParser writes spreadsheets and slides as well as documents: .xlsx, .ods, .pptx and .odp, next to DOCX, ODT, PDF, HTML, Markdown, LaTeX, RTF, EPUB, CSV, plain text and chunks for retrieval. What it writes is what it read: a workbook's values, shown in their number formats, and a deck's text boxes, pictures, shapes, tables and speaker notes.

It does not write formulas, since it never reads them (see section 2), and it writes a chart as a table of its data, on a sheet or a slide, not as a chart Excel or PowerPoint can edit. If the deliverable needs live formulas or editable charts, use a library built for authoring them, such as ExcelJS or PptxGenJS.

5. You Need to Run Macros

Macro-enabled files carry VBA code. officeParser has no VBA runtime. It never executes macro code, and it does not read it or carry it into anything it generates. If your workflow depends on a macro running, you need Office itself.

6. You Need a TeX Engine

officeParser reads LaTeX and writes LaTeX, but it interprets LaTeX. It does not compile it.

Reading a .tex file, it follows the structure the way a converter does: sections, lists, tables, math, footnotes, citations, and the macros you define yourself (\newcommand, \def), which it expands within fixed limits. It does not load packages, so a command from a package it does not know keeps its text. Drawings (TikZ, pgfplots, picture) are left out. And it never typesets, so there are no line breaks, page numbers, or floats placed on a page.

Going the other way, ast.to('tex') gives you source that compiles with pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX, or LuaLaTeX. To turn that source into a camera-ready PDF, you still run a real TeX distribution.

Smaller Limits Worth Knowing

  • Slide reading order. Shapes on a slide are read in the order the file lists them, not sorted by position. The PPTX article explains why that is hard.
  • Untagged PDFs. Without a tag tree, tables and headings are recovered from geometry, which is best-effort. The PDF article has the details.
  • Runtime. The npm package needs Node.js 22.13 or newer.

The Decision Matrix

A summary of how officeParser compares with three tools people often reach for:

Capability officeParser Pandoc LibreOffice (headless) python-docx / openpyxl
What you install An npm package A native binary A full office suite Python packages
Runs in the browser Yes Not as shipped Not as shipped Not as shipped
One document model across formats Yes (typed AST) Yes (Pandoc AST) Only through its UNO API No, one model per library
Chunks for retrieval Built in No No No
Legacy .doc / .xls / .ppt No No Yes No
Formula recalculation No No Yes No
Print layout close to Word No No Closest of the four No

When officeParser is the Right Tool

Reach for it when the job is:

  • Getting documents into a search index, a retrieval pipeline, or an LLM prompt with their structure intact.
  • Converting between Office formats, Markdown, HTML, LaTeX, and PDF from one typed tree.
  • Processing documents in the browser, so a confidential file never leaves the user's machine.
  • Running in a plain Node.js service where you would rather not install and supervise an office suite.

That is the job it was built for. For everything above the line, use the tool built for that job. Knowing where the boundary sits is part of using any library well.

item.title: Document Chunking for Retrieval Done Right: Beyond Naive Token Windows
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: Why a sliding token window shreds tables and orphans headings, what chunking on document structure fixes, and what officeParser's chunker does and does not do.
item.content:encoded:
In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the quality of the answer is bounded by the quality of what was retrieved. If the relevant passage never reaches the context window, no amount of prompt engineering will produce it.

Yet a great many pipelines still ingest documents with some variation of this: 

// The usual first attempt:
const text = extractRawText(file);
const chunks = recursiveTextSplitter(text, {
    chunkSize: 500,
    chunkOverlap: 50,
});

For prose this is tolerable. For office documents, with their tables and nested headings, it loses exactly the parts that matter. Here is why.

The Anatomy of Chunking Failure

A window of fixed size sliding over a string is blind to structure. It cuts wherever the count runs out:

1. The Table Shredder

Take a financial table with a header row and a row per quarter. The window fills up partway through, and the splitter cuts there:

  • Chunk 1 holds the header row and the first three quarters.
  • Chunk 2 starts with: | Q4 | 47,310 | 19.0% |.

Chunk 2 has lost its column names. When someone asks "What was the operating margin in Q4?", the words "operating margin" appear only in chunk 1, so chunk 2 is a poor match for the query. And if it is retrieved anyway, the model has no way to know what 19.0% measures.

2. The Orphaned Heading

A heading is the context for everything under it. A fixed window often leaves the heading at the end of one chunk and its content at the start of the next: 

[End of chunk 24]
... in accordance with regional regulations.
4.2 Data Retention Exceptions

[Start of chunk 25]
Medical records must be archived for a minimum of 7 years.
All audit trails must be immutable.

Retrieve chunk 25 alone and nothing says that "7 years" is about data retention exceptions and not about, say, ordinary log storage.

The Fix: Chunk the Structure, Not the String

Both failures come from the same place: by the time the splitter runs, the structure is already gone. The fix is to chunk before flattening, while a table is still a table and a heading is still a heading.

Three rules for structural chunking
  1. Cut at structural boundaries. Between paragraphs, sections, pages, or slides. Never in the middle of a table row.
  2. Carry the heading. Every chunk should know which heading it sits under, ideally the whole path of headings above it.
  3. Repeat table headers. When a table is too big for one chunk, every piece should start with the header row.

What officeParser's Chunker Does

officeParser parses every format into one tree, so its chunker works on nodes, not characters. You reach it with ast.to('chunks'): 

import { parseOffice } from 'officeparser';

const ast = await parseOffice('service-agreement.docx');

const { value: chunks } = await ast.to('chunks', {
    chunksConfig: {
        strategy: 'document-structure',  // the default
        splitBy: 'heading',  // or 'paragraph', 'page', 'slide', 'sheet'
        maxChunkSize: 1500,
        tableSplitStrategy: 'row',       // repeat the header row
    },
});

Here is real output for a short Markdown document: a paragraph under the heading "3.2 Uptime Credits", followed by a four-row table that I forced to split by setting a small maxChunkSize. The chunks for the headings themselves are left out: 

[
  {
    "text": "If monthly uptime falls below 99.9%, the customer is
             entitled to a 10% credit. Below 99.0%, a 25% credit
             applies.",
    "metadata": {
      "sourceType": "md",
      "closestHeading": "3.2 Uptime Credits"
    }
  },
  {
    "text": "| Quarter | Revenue | Operating margin |
             | Q1 | 41,900 | 16.2% |
             | Q2 | 43,750 | 17.1% |
             | Q3 | 45,200 | 18.4% |",
    "metadata": {
      "sourceType": "md",
      "closestHeading": "3.2 Uptime Credits",
      "isTableChunk": true
    }
  },
  {
    "text": "| Quarter | Revenue | Operating margin |
             | Q4 | 47,310 | 19.0% |",
    "metadata": {
      "sourceType": "md",
      "closestHeading": "3.2 Uptime Credits",
      "isTableChunk": true
    }
  }
]

(The long strings are wrapped here to fit the page.) Measured against the three rules:

  • Rule 1, boundaries: done, with one exception. Chunks follow the tree, and a table is cut between rows. A single row longer than maxChunkSize is cut inside, because no chunk could hold it whole.
  • Rule 3, table headers: done. The second table chunk begins with the header row, so the Q4 figures still have their column names. isTableChunk marks both pieces.
  • Rule 2, headings: partly. Each chunk records its closestHeading, along with pageNumber, slideNumber, or sheetName where the format has them. But it is the nearest heading only, not the full path above it, and it lives in the metadata, not in the text that gets embedded.

Putting the Heading Where the Embedding Can See It

If the heading is only in metadata, the embedding model never sees it. Prepend it yourself. A heading is also emitted as a chunk of its own, so skip the case where a chunk is its heading: 

for (const chunk of chunks) {
    const heading = chunk.metadata.closestHeading;
    const textToEmbed = heading && heading !== chunk.text
        ? `${heading}\n\n${chunk.text}`
        : chunk.text;

    // Embed textToEmbed. Store chunk.metadata next to the vector,
    // for filtering and for citations.
}

Sizes in Tokens, and Other Strategies

Sizes are counted in characters by default. To count tokens, pass a lengthFunction: your tokenizer's counter goes in, and maxChunkSize becomes a token budget.

Two more strategies are there when structure is not what you want. fixed-size is the familiar recursive splitter with overlap. semantic cuts where the topic shifts, using an embedding function that you supply.

Measure It on Your Own Documents

I am not going to quote a benchmark here. Retrieval numbers do not travel well between corpora, and the only result that matters is the one on your documents. What I can offer is the experiment worth running on your own files:

  1. Collect a few dozen real questions, and make sure some can only be answered from a table.
  2. For each question, note which passage of which document holds the answer.
  3. Index the documents twice: once with a fixed-size splitter, once with structural chunks.
  4. For each index, count how often the right passage shows up in the top results.

Pay attention to the table questions. That is where the two approaches differ most, and where a wrong answer is hardest to notice.

Summary

Stop treating documents as strings of characters. The structure an author put into a document is information, and a retrieval pipeline that flattens it first is working with less than it was given.

Cut at boundaries, keep tables whole or repeat their headers, and make sure every chunk knows where in the document it came from.
